title: Freya and the Colony
premise: Beatrix Almeida, a xenolinguist whose dreams have been colonized by an alien grammar, tends a forgotten beacon on the fringe of human space. When the long-lost ship Meridian returns with its crew aged backward into children who speak only in that same alien tongue, Beatrix realizes his own linguistic drift is not illness but infection—and that the beacon has been calling something toward humanity for decades. Racing a rival faction that wants to weaponize the signal, he must reach the dead-space relay and choose between silencing it forever or answering it, discovering in the process that the 'colony' is a distributed mind offering survival at the cost of selfhood. In the end, Beatrix answers—but on his own terms, translating rather than surrendering, becoming a bridge instead of a doorway.
about_author: Yara Fairweather is a former radio astronomer turned novelist who writes first-contact fiction from a converted lighthouse on the Atlantic coast. Her work explores what language does to the people who carry it.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. We meet him maintaining the ancient relay beacon on station Kestrel-9, logging signals no one reads, dreaming nightly in a syntax that isn't human. He's isolated, disciplined, quietly frightened of his own mind. Beat: loneliness as routine.

chapters.title: Grammar of the Dark
chapters.summary: Beatrix decodes a new pattern in the beacon's traffic—identical to his dream-language. He files a report to Earth and receives an automated rejection. Emotional beat: creeping dread as work and nightmare merge.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: A derelict ship appears at the edge of sensor range: the Meridian, lost forty years ago. Its crew are children—the original adults de-aged, alive, speaking fluent alien. POV shifts to Wren, a seven-year-old with a sixty-year-old's eyes. Beat: uncanny wonder.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Way Home
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The child-crew remembers everything but experiences it through new brains. Wren recognizes Beatrix's dream-speech instantly and calls him 'half-turned.' Beat: recognition and fear of kinship.

chapters.title: Quarantine of One
chapters.summary: Beatrix locks down the station, torn between studying the children and protecting himself. He records Wren's speech and finds his own unconscious utterances match it. Beat: denial cracking.

chapters.title: The Company Men
chapters.summary: POV: Commander Ilse Varga, arriving aboard the corporate vessel Persephone, ordered to seize the Meridian and the beacon. She sees the children as assets. Beat: cold ambition entering a fragile ecosystem.

chapters.title: What the Signal Wants
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Wren decode the beacon's full message: an invitation, repeating for decades—an offer of merger from a distributed intelligence calling itself the Colony. Beat: revelation reframing everything.

chapters.title: Varga's Bargain
chapters.summary: Varga offers Beatrix passage home in exchange for the translation keys. He refuses; she takes the child-crew anyway. Beat: power corrupting, helplessness.

chapters.title: Half-Turned
chapters.summary: Alone again, Beatrix stops suppressing the dream-language and lets it surface deliberately, mapping its logic. He discovers it encodes memory across generations—immortality by distribution. Beat: temptation.

chapters.title: Theft of Small Voices
chapters.summary: Wren's POV aboard Persephone. The children resist Varga's tests by speaking only in Colony-tongue, which terrifies the crew. Wren smuggles a message to Beatrix via the beacon. Beat: resistance.

chapters.title: Dead Space Ahead
chapters.summary: Beatrix steals a maintenance skiff and pursues Persephone toward the relay at the edge of dead space, where the signal originates. His body begins changing—he hears the Colony while awake. Beat: commitment, point of no return.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Varga's POV. Corporate command orders her to detonate the relay, sacrificing the children's cure to contain the threat. She hesitates—then complies. Beat: corruption completing itself.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Beatrix reaches the relay first and finds it isn't machinery—it's a dormant node of the Colony itself, grown from something ancient. It speaks to him directly, in his mother's voice. Beat: awe and horror.

chapters.title: Terms of Survival
chapters.summary: The Colony offers Beatrix everything: restoration of the Meridian crew, endless life, an end to loneliness—for total dissolution of individual identity. He asks for time. Beat: the price made explicit.

chapters.title: Countdown
chapters.summary: Persephone arrives; Varga arms the charges. Beatrix broadcasts Wren's smuggled testimony to her crew, sowing doubt about what they're destroying. Beat: tension peak, moral pressure.

chapters.title: Mutiny of Conscience
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The children stage a desperate escape during the standoff; two are killed. Wren reaches Beatrix, and their joined languages briefly open a window into the Colony's true nature—it is afraid too. Beat: grief and empathy.

chapters.title: Varga's Choice
chapters.summary: Varga, confronted with the dying children and the Colony's genuine offer to restore them, must choose obedience or mercy. She stands down the charges—but her superiors launch an automated failsafe. Beat: redemption too late to be simple.

chapters.title: The Answering
chapters.summary: Climax. With minutes before the failsafe strike, Beatrix enters the relay node and negotiates in both tongues at once—not surrender, but translation: humanity will speak with the Colony, not dissolve into it. The Colony accepts a boundary. Beat: sacrifice and triumph.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: The strike destroys half the relay; the surviving node goes quiet but not silent. The Meridian children begin aging forward again, restored. Beatrix wakes human—or nearly. Beat: exhausted relief.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: En route home, Beatrix records his full report, knowing Earth will twist it. Varga, disgraced but alive, chooses to testify with him against corporate containment policy. Beat: accountability.

chapters.title: Dreams in Two Tongues
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Months later, the dreams have changed—they're now conversations, bilingual, consensual. He teaches the first class of human-Colony linguistics. Beat: integration without erasure.

chapters.title: Freya and the Colony
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Wren's POV years later. Wren, now grown, names the Colony 'Freya' after the beacon's forgotten commission file—and reveals the beacon was built by humans who answered once before, long ago. The dialogue continues. Beat: hope with open eyes.
